snapshot if you switch that on.
Link. The notes live elsewhere — typically in a vault.
Writing happens there, in Obsidian; Quartz reads through the link. The project then contains not one
note, only the reference to them.
If the path is followed by “(target does not exist)”, the vault has been moved, renamed, or is on
a drive that is not mounted. The link itself is still there; it just points nowhere.
What the link means for snapshots
A linked vault is not backed up. The snapshot holds the link, not a single note. The app says so
explicitly on the backups page, and it is not a defect but the right division of labour: the vault is
a source of its own with a backup of its own — and a snapshot would never overwrite it anyway.
Anyone wanting both backs up the vault themselves: with a repository of its own, with Obsidian Sync,
or with whatever else.
Changing the source
Change source… opens a dialog with two fields: the new source folder and the strategy.

Two fields, and above them the sentence that nothing is deleted.

















StrategyWhat happensLinkcontent/ becomes a reference to the chosen folder. Nothing is copied.CopyThe chosen folder’s content is copied in once; content/ becomes a real folder.
Above both stands the sentence that matters:

The previous content folder is set aside rather than deleted before the change — you can bring it
back under Backups.

So nothing is lost. The old folder moves to a place inside the project that the backups page
knows about, and from there it can be brought back or deleted for good (see
7.4).
When copying, the app shows the progress in files — with a large vault that takes a while.
What does not work
The source folder must not lie inside the project’s content folder. That one is set aside first
when switching — so the source would move along while being copied from. The app refuses and says so.
After the switch
Two things pay off:

Check the wikilink setting. How the targets are written — shortest form, absolute, relative —
has to match the new notes, or the links find nothing.
Rebuild, so the preview shows the new content.

en/3-setup/05-translations.title: 3.5 Translations
en/3-setup/05-translations.content:
A Quartz site contains text that does not come from the notes: “Search”, “Last updated”, “Graph
view”, “Back”. It comes from Quartz’s language files. The Translations tab makes it editable.

The site’s fixed wording, per language.
Which language applies is decided by the
Site tab instead.
What is here
On the left the languages the project brings; on the right their entries, with a search over keys and
text. Editing happens straight in the field; the top shows how many changes are still unsaved.
If the app finds no language files at all, it says so (quartz/i18n/locales missing) — then something
fundamental is wrong with this project.
Core text only. Whatever an individual plugin brings in text of its own does not appear here.
The “JS” badge
Some entries are not fixed text but building blocks filled with values at build time — “3 days ago”,
“5 results”. They carry the badge JS.
They can be edited like the others, but the structure inside has to stay: remove the place where the
number is inserted and you get a text without a number.
The update protection
At the top it says Update protection active or Update protection not active, and there is a
real problem behind that.
Your own wording lives in Quartz’s own files. A core update fetches new versions of those files —
and would take your changes with it. The protection makes sure that does not happen.
It is set up automatically on the next save; to have it beforehand, press Enable now. Anyone
with wording of their own and without the protection should see to it before the next
update.
What this has to do with templates
Changed wording is one of the twelve parts of a
template package — so it travels along when a design
is handed on. On export you can choose whether all texts come along or only the changed ones. The
latter needs a baseline for comparison, and that comes about only once you have edited a text in this
app; see 4.9.

en/3-setup/index.title: 3 Setup
en/3-setup/index.content:
Everything a site knows about itself lives here: what it is called, what address it will be reachable
at, which language its fixed wording appears in, and where its notes come from.
The pages of this chapter

3.1 The overview — a project’s status page and what its tiles mean.
3.2 Title, address and behaviour — page title, base
URL, language, exclusions, analytics.
3.3 The project image — the picture in the project list that
doubles as the site’s favicon.
3.4 The content folder — a real folder or a link to an
Obsidian vault, and how to switch between them without losing anything.
3.5 Translations — changing the site’s fixed wording and carrying
it through a core update.

The plugins also sit under Setup in the sidebar, but under 4.8 in this
handbook — because that is where what they do on the finished page is explained.

en/4-design/01-the-four-layers.title: 4.1 The four layers
en/4-design/01-the-four-layers.content:
The Styles area has four tabs, and their order is not a matter of taste: it is exactly the order
in which the four layers override one another.
Base  →  Community theme  →  Variables  →  custom CSS
                                           wins


The four tabs stand in the order in which they override one another; the line below says what
currently applies.
That line is in the app too, above the tabs, and it names which theme is active.
What each layer does
Base — the nine base colours and the three font roles, for light and dark. That is the layer
Quartz works with on its own. Everything beyond is optional.
Community theme — a finished colour scheme from
outside. While one is active it overrides the base colours; the base values stay stored and apply
again as soon as the theme is off. That is why they are dimmed rather than locked in the Base tab,
with the count beside them: “The theme overrides 7 of 9 colours and 2 of 3 fonts.”
Variables — overriding individual values on purpose,
including ones neither base nor theme offers. That is the route when a theme almost fits.
Custom CSS — everything the three layers above cannot express. Beats everything else.
The rule of thumb
Work from the top down. Whatever the Base tab can set belongs there; only what is missing there
becomes a variable; only what a variable cannot do either becomes custom CSS.
The reason is not tidiness: every layer further down is one more place a later theme or an update
cannot reach through. A colour set in the Base tab follows the colour scheme; the same colour in
custom CSS stays put even when it no longer fits.
The exception worth knowing
A theme can set colours that apply only to one kind of element — a callout’s colour, say. Such
values cannot be overridden globally in the Variables tab; that needs custom CSS. The app says so
where it becomes relevant.
Known conflicts
Below the tabs is a card called Known conflicts. It lists cases where two
plugins get in each other’s way and no setting resolves it —
only CSS.
Press Create fix and you get an ordinary file under Custom CSS: editable, movable, deletable
like any other. The app hides nothing; it only writes down what you would otherwise have to work out
yourself.

en/4-design/02-base-colours-and-fonts.title: 4.2 Base — colours and fonts
en/4-design/02-base-colours-and-fonts.content:
The Base tab is the lowest of the four layers. Here are the
values Quartz works with on its own.
Colours
Nine colours, once for light and once for dark. They are not decoration: Quartz derives a whole set
of further variables from them — which ones and how is
shown by the Variables tab.
If a community theme is active, the colours it
overrides are dimmed, with the count above them. They can still be edited — the values apply
again as soon as the theme is off.
Fonts
Three roles: headings, body text and code. A font family for each.
Above them is the font source, and with it the question of where the font comes from:

Google Fonts — Quartz fetches it from there. How it is then delivered is decided by the switch
below.
Brought yourself — Quartz fetches nothing; the font has to be in the project, for instance
through the import further down.

Font delivery

The switch sits below the three font roles; the line beneath it says what currently applies.
The switch Serve fonts locally is the most important one on this page once the site goes public.

Off: the finished page links Google Fonts. Every visit calls Google.
On: Quartz downloads the font files once at build time and puts them in the project. The
page then calls nobody else — the privacy-friendly variant.



                  
                  This needs a base URL 
                  
                

The font URLs are rewritten onto it. Without it the build fails. It is set under
Configuration → Base URL.


Below it, one line says what actually applies right now — whether the Quartz core or the “Fonts”
plugin delivers the fonts, and whether linked or local.
The theme’s own fonts
If the active theme brings fonts of its own, it loads them from unpkg.com — that is a third-party
call too, and it cannot be served locally. It stays a decision:

Theme fonts on: designed as intended, at the cost of a call to unpkg.
Theme fonts off: no call, but the font roles from above take over, and the theme looks
different from how it was meant to.

Importing a font of your own
Takes a .ttf, .otf, .woff or .woff2 from the filesystem, puts it in the project and writes the
matching rule into the custom CSS. Optionally it can be assigned to one of the three roles right
away.
The app reads the font weight out of the file and says what it found — including when it found
nothing: “The file names no weight, so the rule stays without one.” The font is then available,
but without a statement of whether it is bold or light.

en/4-design/03-community-themes.title: 4.3 Community themes
en/4-design/03-community-themes.content:
A community theme is a finished colour scheme from
outside. It sits in the second of the four layers: it overrides the
base colours, and is overridden in turn by variables and custom CSS.

The catalogue of community themes.
The catalogue
At the bottom of the page. Searchable (tokyo-night, catppuccin, nord …), with details for every
entry: which modes exist, which variations, whether custom colours can be adjusted, which fonts come
along.
Install & activate fetches the theme and sets it. Afterwards the message contains a sentence
worth taking seriously: do not forget to click “Save” at the top. It is installed immediately, but
recorded only on saving.
If the list cannot be loaded, the app says so and shows only a few well-known themes as placeholders.
That is pointedly not the statement “there are no more” — try again with Reload. A
GitHub token in the settings helps if the request limit is the
cause.
The active theme
At the top is which one applies. Below it, that theme’s own settings — but only the ones the theme
itself brings.
If it brings none, the app says so plainly and adds the reason: that is down to the theme, not to
this app. Values of your own would simply be ignored by Quartz at that point. Anyone wanting to
change something anyway does so in the Variables tab or in the custom
CSS — a link leads straight there.
For many themes there are also descriptions of the individual options, fetched from the original
theme. Where they are missing, the switches stand bare — the app says that too, instead of inventing
names.
Presets
A preset is a saved set: a base theme plus your own changes to it, under a name. The route to one:

Install and activate a theme from the catalogue.
Adjust it at the top.
Save as preset, with a name.

After that, several can be kept side by side and switched between with one click — useful for
comparing two colour worlds without losing the first.
Switching off
Disable community themes switches all of it off. The classic theme from the
base layer applies again.
The settings are kept. Switching off is not deleting; a click on Re-enable restores the state.

en/4-design/04-variables.title: 4.4 Variables
en/4-design/04-variables.content:
A CSS variable is a named value the stylesheets use in
many places. The Variables tab is the third of the four layers:
what is here beats the base and the theme.

The main variables, with the count of overrides.
Main variables
The variables Quartz derives from the nine base colours. Every row unfolds, and then shows two
things:

Where the value comes from — the chain back to the base colour.
What depends on it — how many other variables change along with it.

The second is the more important one. When it says “A value of your own here affects 6 further
variables”, that is not a warning but a piece of information: you are not changing one colour, you
are changing a family.
Every variable has a value for light and one for dark, and every one can be reset to its original
value individually. The counter at the top says how many of how many are overridden.
All theme and build variables
The second card. It holds everything the active theme, the plugins or the last
build bring in variables — kept apart from the main variables,
because there can be a great many.
That is why there is a search first and a list second. A filter Changed only shows what you
touched yourself.
If it says “There is no build output yet”, the source is simply missing: build once, then
Reload.
What does not work here
Some variables are set by a theme only inside a particular element — a callout’s colours, say.
Such values cannot be overridden globally here, and the row says so: “cannot be resolved (set only
inside a selector)”. That needs custom CSS.
When variables are the right place
When a theme almost fits. Changing a single colour in it without giving up the whole theme happens
exactly here — and stays readable, because a counter says how many deviations there are by now.
If you find yourself overriding more than a handful of values, the theme is usually the wrong one.

en/4-design/05-custom-css.title: 4.5 Custom CSS
en/4-design/05-custom-css.content:
The fourth and last of the four layers. What is here beats
everything else — and is therefore also the layer a later theme cannot reach past.

Custom CSS: the load order on the left, the editor on the right.
The load order
Quartz includes one file only: custom.scss. Everything else is loaded from there. The card
Load order shows that chain and makes it editable:

Move up / move down — files loaded later override earlier ones.
New file, Rename, Delete.
custom.scss itself is always last and cannot be moved.

Below it a second list may appear: Present but not included. Those are files in the stylesheet
folder that nobody loads — after a rearrangement by hand, for instance. A click on Include hooks
them into the chain.
Several files instead of one big one pay off for the same reason as everywhere: you find again what
you were looking for. The example template shows how — one file per component.
The check
Check code compiles what you wrote without building. Two answers:

“SCSS compiles without errors.”
“SCSS error — the build would fail”, with a file and a line number and a link that jumps
straight there.

That is the check that saves you a failed build. Its result turns
up again on the overview — and there also the third state: CSS
unchecked, which means neither “good” nor “bad”.
The helpers for writing

The callout variables, with the real values from the current state.
Pick component inserts the selector for an element of the page at the cursor — so you need not
know what the explorer is called in the HTML.
Colours currently in effect and Fonts currently in effect show what applies right now, light
and dark, with a font sample. A click inserts the name as a variable reference, a click on a colour
swatch inserts the value.
For the fonts, “not installed” may appear beside one, and the app explains what that means: the
font is not present on this machine, and the app fetches nothing from the network — so the sample
shows the fallback, not the real thing. On the finished site it may still look right.
Original styles (read-only) shows what Quartz itself writes. For looking up, not for changing.
When two tabs touch the same file
custom.scss is not written here only: a variable override and a font import land in it as well. If
another tab changed the file while an unsaved draft is here, the app says so — saving would
overwrite that change — and offers to reload from disk.
When custom CSS is the right place
When there is no other. Three cases regularly are:

Values a theme sets only inside a particular element (callout colours, say) — marked cannot be
resolved in the Variables tab.
Structure rather than colour: spacings, borders, line breaks.
The known conflicts, for which the app creates the fix as an
ordinary file here.

en/4-design/06-layout-frames.title: 4.6 Layout — frames
en/4-design/06-layout-frames.content:
A frame is a page’s grid: which areas exist — header,
sidebars, content, footer —, where they sit and how wide they are.

A freshly created frame: two by two cells, and all seven areas still in the list below.
Three things are to be kept apart, and they live in three tabs:





















QuestionWhereHow is the page divided?Own frames — this pageWhat appears in which area?Tab Global, see 4.7Which page type uses which grid?Tab Page types, same place
Quartz brings three frames — default, full-width, minimal. Here you build your own.
The editor

An area is dragged from the list onto a cell; it stays behind pale in its place.
On the left are the areas without a place yet; on the right the grid. Dragging an area onto a free
cell places it; dragging a placed area back into the list frees it again. A click selects an area
and shows its settings below — among them how many rows and columns it spans.
This works with the keyboard too: pick up with space or enter, move with the arrow keys, drop
with space or enter, cancel with escape. The app announces what happens as you go.
Changes take effect immediately in the editor’s preview — saving still happens only on Save.
Three widths
Every frame of your own is built for three screen widths: desktop, tablet, phone. The switch at the
top moves between them; each has a grid of its own.
Each width has a box: a maximum width, an alignment and inner padding. Two subtleties about it
are in the editor:

Without a maximum width the box uses the full window width.
The alignment only takes effect with a maximum width — before that there is nothing left to
distribute.

Breakpoints
At which window width it switches to tablet or phone is a field of its own. The default is 1200 /
800 — the same values Quartz uses.
Two limits the app names: the values apply to this project’s own frames. Quartz’s built-in frames
and community themes bring values of their own and do not follow these.
Naming lines
A field in the editor names the lines between columns and rows. The editor does not need this —
areas are placed by dragging. It is only useful if you later want to address those lines from
custom CSS.
Frames a plugin brings
Some plugins bring a frame of their own for their own kind of
page. For those the editor shows no preview, and that is meant honestly: only the plugin knows how
such a frame is built.
Where frames turn up elsewhere
Quartz registers every frame of your own as a plugin — which is
why they also appear in the plugin list. They are still configured here; the list there says so too.

en/4-design/07-layout-global-and-page-ty.title: 4.7 Layout — global and page types
en/4-design/07-layout-global-and-page-ty.content:
The Global tab: the page’s areas on the left, the components without a place yet on the right.
Frames say where the areas sit. The other two tabs say what is in
them and for which pages that holds.
Global
A board with the page’s areas — header, left and right sidebar, before and after the content, footer.
Into each area you drag the components that should appear there:
explorer, search, table of contents, backlinks, graph, theme switcher and so on.
Dragging works with the mouse and with the keyboard (space to pick up, arrow keys to move, space to
drop, escape to cancel). An empty area says so itself: “Empty — drag here”.
Every placed component carries two settings:

Visibility — always, desktop only, mobile only.
Group — see below.

Flex groups
Without a group every component stands on its own, one below the other. Components with the same
group stand side by side — or stacked, reversed, with a gap, in an order that can be set.
That is the route to a header in which the title, the search and the switcher sit in one row instead
of three.
Page types
Quartz distinguishes kinds of page: content pages, folder pages, tag pages, canvas
pages, bases pages and the 404 page. The Page types tab lets each depart from the global
layout.
Two things can be set per page type:
Frame — which grid this page type uses: default, full-width, minimal, or one of your own.
Visible components — which components are hidden on pages of this type. A tag page needs no table
of contents; the 404 page perhaps no sidebar at all.
A page type with departures carries the badge Customised, and Remove override resets it to the
global layout.


                  
                  Duplicate components 
                  
                

If the same component is placed more than once, switching it off affects all of its instances.
The app says so with the count; Quartz cannot separate individual duplicates at this point.


The preview
At the top you can pick which page type the grid structure is shown for — including a note of which
frame currently applies. For a frame a plugin brings, the preview stays empty: only the plugin knows
how it is built.

en/4-design/08-plugins.title: 4.8 Plugins
en/4-design/08-plugins.content:
Quartz consists of plugins. Almost everything visible on the
finished page comes from one: the explorer on the left, the search, the table of contents, the
backlinks, the graph.

The installed plugins, grouped by effect.
In the sidebar the area sits under Setup. In this handbook it is here, because it belongs to the
design: switching a plugin on or off changes how the site looks.
Installed
The list is split into three groups, and the split answers the first question you have about an
unknown plugin — can you see that?
Own frames come first when there are any. They are the grids built in the
layout editor: Quartz registers each as a plugin — which is why they
are here — but they are configured there. A link leads across.
Visible components. They appear on the page: in the header, in the sidebar, in the footer. Where
they appear is decided by the layout editor, not by
this list.
Processing. They change the content behind the scenes — formatting, links, images — and are not
visible themselves. Below them, separated again, the page types: plugins that produce a kind of
page of their own, tag pages for instance.
Configuring
Every row unfolds and shows the plugin’s options. Where Quartz ships a description, the name, type and
explanation come with it.
For bundled plugins Quartz ships none. The app says so instead of inventing options: existing
values can be changed, further ones added by hand — the names are in the plugin’s repository, and a
button opens it.
Sorting
The order in this list is the order in which Quartz runs the plugins, and for processing plugins that
can matter. Reordering is done by dragging — with the mouse or with the keyboard, for which every row
additionally carries move up and move down.
While a filter or a search is active, reordering is switched off. Otherwise a drag would move the
entries you cannot currently see as well.
Removing
Removing a plugin asks first — adding that a snapshot is taken
automatically beforehand. The same holds for a frame of your own, where the file additionally
disappears from disk.
Maintenance
The last card concerns the built files of plugins installed from a source — not what the site can
do. Those files do not belong in the repository and are
therefore missing on a second machine.

Restore from quartz.lock.json — fetches them back. That is the button for “freshly cloned,
plugins missing”.
Remove orphaned plugin folders — deletes whatever no configuration points at any more. The
configuration itself is left unchanged.

Marketplace
The second tab: the catalogue of the quartz-community organisation, searchable, with the bundled
plugins in it. Plugins from elsewhere are added via owner/repo.
If the catalogue is unreachable — GitHub not answering, or the request limit exhausted — the app says
so and shows only a placeholder. A GitHub token in the
settings raises the limit considerably.
A second list holds repositories of the organisation without the “quartz-plugin” marker — among
them Quartz itself, shared libraries and forks. Mostly not installable as a plugin; they are there so
the search does not stay silent when you look for them.

en/4-design/09-template-packages.title: 4.9 Template packages
en/4-design/09-template-packages.content:
A template package is a single file ending in .qtpl.
It holds a project’s design: colours, theme, stylesheets, fonts, layout, frames, plugins,
translations. After importing it into another project, everything there is set as it is here.

Exporting and importing a template package.
The twelve parts
A package is not one unit but twelve. On export and on import, every
part can be picked or left out individually:
Colours and fonts · community theme · plugins · layout · frames · presets · translations ·
stylesheets · fonts · static files · CSS variables · content.
The last is the special one: the notes themselves. For most templates you do not want that — a
template is a design. For one that explains itself, you do.
Exporting
Everything the project has is selected to begin with; whatever is missing does not appear at all. Each
part states what it contributes — number of files, size.
For the translations there is an extra question: all texts or only
the changed ones. The latter needs a baseline for comparison, and that comes about only once you
have edited a text in this app. If it is missing for a language, the app says so and recommends “All
texts”.
Two size limits are built in, and both have the same sentence behind them: a template is a design,
not a media library and not a backup. If the static files or the content are too large, the app
names the part to take out.
Importing
Before importing, the app shows a preview: what each part would do, how many files would be new,
how many existing ones replaced, and what is skipped.
That preview is the point of the whole feature. It answers the question you have before the click —
what do I lose? — before anything happens. Only then is it applied, and even then a
snapshot is taken first.
What a package may not do
A .qtpl is a file somebody handed on — the app treats it accordingly. Two limits are noticeable as a
user:
A template writes nothing into a linked content folder. If content/ is a
link to a vault, the content
part is skipped, and the app says why: pouring somebody else’s notes into your own vault could not be
undone.
No part writes outside the project. Every filename from the package is checked before it is
touched.
The bundled template
QuartzControl brings a finished template — the same one the wizard offers when a project is created.
It can be imported afterwards at any time, for instance if you left it out then or if the import went
wrong.

en/4-design/index.title: 4 Design
en/4-design/index.content:
The largest chapter, because this is where most of the time goes. It follows the order in which the
four layers override one another: base, community theme, variables, custom CSS.
The pages of this chapter

4.1 The four layers — who beats whom, and why the tabs are in
this order.
4.2 Base: colours and fonts — the nine colours, the
three font roles, light and dark, and where the fonts come from.
4.3 Community themes — installing, activating, adjusting,
saving as a preset.
4.4 Variables — what a CSS variable is, where its value comes from
and what depends on it.
4.5 Custom CSS — the files, their load order, and the check before
the build.
4.6 Layout: frames — building a page’s grid, for three screen
widths.
4.7 Layout: global and page types — what appears
in which area, and which page type uses which grid.
4.8 Plugins — configuring and sorting installed plugins, finding new
ones in the marketplace.
4.9 Template packages — handing a design on as a file, and
taking on somebody else’s.

en/5-preview-and-build/01-the-preview.title: 5.1 The preview
en/5-preview-and-build/01-the-preview.content:
The dev server builds the site, serves it locally and
rebuilds on every change to a note. That is the state you write in.

Preview & build: dev server, servers found, one-off build.
Starting
On Preview & build, or straight from the overview. Afterwards it
says since when it has been running and on which port.
Two settings beside it can only be changed while the server is stopped — the app says so too:

Port and WS port — the second is the channel the page reloads itself over.
Remote dev host — only needed when the preview should be reachable through a tunnel.

Looking at it
Two ways:

In the browser, at http://localhost:<port>.
In the live preview right in the app, with a width switch: desktop, tablet, mobile, full width.
That is the quick way to see whether a frame still works on a
phone.


The running server with the live preview in the app — here showing this handbook.
Below it is the dev server’s output. It is not decoration: when a note contains an error or a
plugin complains, that is where it says so.
When it stops
If the server exits unexpectedly, the app says so with the exit code, and the
overview reports it under Needs attention. The reason is almost always
in the output above — an error in the custom CSS is the most common.
It does not belong to the window
A running server survives leaving the project, and if you want it, quitting the app — what happens
then is set in the settings under On quit. The start screen shows
for every project whether one is running.
That is intended: closing the app does not necessarily mean giving up the preview somebody is reading
in the browser.

en/5-preview-and-build/02-the-build.title: 5.2 The build
en/5-preview-and-build/02-the-build.content:
A build produces the finished site once — the HTML files, the
stylesheets, the search index, the images. Afterwards a folder sits there that can be uploaded,
checked or handed on.
For looking at things while writing there is the
dev server. The build is the step before publishing.
What is there afterwards

After the build: result, duration, and the output below.
The card shows when the last build was and how many files are in the output folder — or “Never
built”. A button opens the folder.
Below it the build output, with the result and the duration: Successful in 4 s or Failed. On
failure the reason is above it.
The output folder
The default is public/ in the project. Anyone changing it should have read two sentences that are in
the app as well:

Every build empties this folder first.


Also used by Publish — the upload comes from the same folder.

The first is the important one. A build is not an addition but a replacement; whatever was in there
before is gone afterwards.
That is why the app checks the folder before using it. If it holds files that do not look like a
build, it says so with the count and asks:

It holds 12 entries that do not look like a Quartz build. Every build wipes its output folder
completely — this cannot be undone.

And some folders it refuses outright — the project folder itself, for instance. It then names the
reason and suggests a folder of its own.
When a build pays off although the server is running
Three cases:

Before publishing. What gets uploaded is the content of the output folder — not what the dev
server currently holds in memory.
To read in variables. The Variables tab can show what the theme
and the plugins actually produce — for which it needs a build.
To check. A build reports errors the server passes over when building incrementally.

en/5-preview-and-build/03-reading-the-co.title: 5.3 Reading the console
en/5-preview-and-build/03-reading-the-co.content:
Below the preview and below the build sits a console each. It shows what Quartz says — verbatim,
untranslated, because it is another program’s output.
What is normal

A successful build: four lines, plus the result and the duration above them.
A successful run looks roughly like this:
Found 52 input files from `content`
Parsed 52 Markdown files in 304ms
Filtered out 0 files
Emitted 249 files to `public` in 4s

Four lines, four questions: how many files were found, how many read, how many removed by the
exclusion patterns, how many written.
The first number is the most useful one. If it is far too small, the
content folder does not point where you think it does.
The common errors

























What it saysWhat is behind itbad indentation of a mapping entryA frontmatter value with a colon that is not in quotes. The build breaks off at the first affected file.An SCSS error with a line numberThe custom CSS cannot be compiled. The tab there checks that without building.Cannot find moduleThe dependencies are missing — typical for a freshly cloned project.A plugin reporting by nameThen it is that plugin’s message; the plugin’s repository is the right address.
When the preview does not start
Almost always the port is taken. The card Servers running on this machine says whether something
is already there — see 5.4. If the port is
taken but by no recognisable Quartz server, the app says that too: a start on this port will fail.
When the output stays empty
In rare cases the app reports that it cannot record the server’s output. The server still runs —
only this console stays empty for this run. In the browser the preview is reachable as usual.

en/5-preview-and-build/04-servers-that-a.title: 5.4 Servers that are not the app's
en/5-preview-and-build/04-servers-that-a.content:
More than one Quartz server can run on a machine: one from this app, one from a terminal, one from a
session that was killed. The card Servers running on this machine looks for them and lists them.

The detection, here with nothing found.
What is in the list
Per entry the port, the project — as far as it can be recognised — and the origin:

From this app — started by QuartzControl.
Started outside — by something else.

Plus whether the server answers a request. A process that is still there but no longer answers is
a different case from none at all.
“Unknown” is not “none”
On some systems the process list cannot be read. The app then says exactly that:

The process list cannot be read on this system. Whether servers are running is unknown —
not “none”.

The same attitude as everywhere in this app: what cannot be determined does not become an all-clear.
Stopping is a decision every time
The app never stops a foreign server on its own. The sentence on the card says why:

Servers started outside this app belong to someone else — a terminal, a second window, a session
that was force-quit.

It asks accordingly differently. For a server of its own: the preview in the browser will no longer
be reachable. For a foreign one: whoever started it may be working with it right now.
At startup
If the app finds servers left over from an earlier session at startup, it asks once what should
happen to them. Whether it does depends on the setting
*On quit*: choose “Keep running” and you get this question on the
next start.
Why stopping sometimes does not work
If it then says “could not be stopped”, there are two possibilities, and the app names both: the
server was already gone — or the process number now belongs to somebody else. Operating systems reuse
numbers, and between showing a list and clicking on it lies any amount of time. That is why the app
checks again immediately before the signal that the number really means the same program.

en/5-preview-and-build/index.title: 5 Preview and build
en/5-preview-and-build/index.content:
Between “written” and “published” comes looking at it. This chapter explains the two ways there —
the server that rebuilds on every change, and the one-off build whose result is uploaded later.
The pages of this chapter

5.1 The preview — starting the server, looking at it in
the browser, stopping it again.
5.2 The build — what it produces, where it lands, and why
the output folder is a serious question.
5.3 Reading the console — which messages are
normal and which are not.
5.4 Servers that are not the app’s — what
the detection finds and why it never stops anything on its own.

en/6-publishing/01-connections-and-targe.title: 6.1 Connections and targets
en/6-publishing/01-connections-and-targe.content:
Publishing takes two things, and they live in two different places. Understand that once and
everything else follows by itself.

Publishing with three targets; the chosen one shows its connection and the server path.

























ConnectionTargetWhatThe login with a provider: server, user, password or key.Where this project publishes to: path, deletion behaviour, exclusions.Belongs tothe appthis projectLives inSettings → ConnectionsPublish
The reason for the split: the same webspace account can carry several sites. A password change is then
one change rather than one per project.
Conversely that means: a duplicate of a project inherits the
connections (those belong to the app) but pointedly not the targets — otherwise it would overwrite
the original’s site with the first click.
Creating a target
+ New target. The form asks for a name and a type, and the type decides the rest:





























TypeFor whatSFTP / rsyncA webspace or your own server, see 6.4FTPThe same, older and unencrypted — same placeFolderA folder on this machine, see 6.5Git branchGitHub Pages, Codeberg Pages and relatives, see 6.2WebhookThe provider builds it itself, see 6.6
A target has exactly one connection, and the type of connection follows from the type of target.
The form therefore offers only matching ones; others are created in the settings.
Deleting a target leaves the connection alone — the app says so in the question.
The host key
For SFTP and rsync the connection shows whether the
host key has been confirmed. On first connecting, the app
shows the server’s fingerprint and asks you to compare it with the one the provider states.
Connect only if they match.
If the key changes later, the transfer breaks off and the app says both things it can mean: a freshly
set-up server — or an attack. Ask first, then Forget host key, never the other way round.
Before you start
If the base URL is still localhost, the page warns at the
top. The finished pages otherwise contain links to localhost — they do not work on the server.

en/6-publishing/02-github-pages.title: 6.2 GitHub Pages
en/6-publishing/02-github-pages.content:
GitHub Pages is the route QuartzControl accompanies furthest: creating a repository, setting up a
target, configuring Pages, a custom domain, HTTPS — all from within the app.
That needs a GitHub token with the repo permission in the
settings.
1. A repository
If there is none yet, Git sync creates one: a name, public or private, and it is entered as
origin right away.


                  
                  Private and Pages do not go together on the free plan 
                  
                

GitHub Pages exists for private repositories only on the paid plans. Anyone publishing via Pages
needs a public repository on the free plan. That can be changed on GitHub later.


2. A target of type “Git branch”
Provider GitHub, plus the branch published to — usually
gh-pages.
Not the branch you work on. A deploy replaces the target branch wholesale with the current build;
the app asks about this explicitly before every deploy and refuses the current or the default branch.
3. Setting up Pages
The GitHub Pages card reads the state directly from GitHub and shows four states: Published,
Building, Failed, Never built.
If Pages is not set up for the repository yet, a button creates it and points it at this branch. If
origin does not point at github.com, the app says so and refers to Git sync — from here it will not
work then.
4. Custom domain and HTTPS
Custom domain records the address with GitHub, not in the branch. That is the decisive difference
from a CNAME file: it survives every deploy, even though a deploy replaces the branch wholesale.
Enforce HTTPS can only be switched on once GitHub has issued the certificate — which takes a few
minutes after setting the domain. Try too early and the app says exactly that, suggesting you try
again later.
Without a custom domain the switch is locked, and that too with a reason: an address on github.io is
always served over HTTPS anyway.
Other providers on the same route
The “Git branch” target knows three providers, and the app says for each what happens afterwards:

GitHub — in the repository settings, Pages must point at this branch.
Codeberg — serves the pages branch directly; after the first push the site is reachable with
no further settings.
GitLab — the branch alone publishes nothing there. A CI job has to deliver the files as a
public artifact. The push works all the same, only nothing follows on its own.

en/6-publishing/03-git-sync.title: 6.3 Git sync
en/6-publishing/03-git-sync.content:
Git sync reconciles the project, not the site. It uploads what lies in the project folder — the
configuration, the stylesheets, and the notes if they are there — so that a second machine can carry
on with it.

Git sync: the state of the repository, here without an “origin”.
Getting the finished site onto a server is the job of
targets. And getting an earlier state back is the job
of snapshots. Three things, three pages.
The state of the repository
At the top is where the project currently stands, and the answers are more precise than “fine”:





































StateWhat it meansUp to date with the remoteNothing to do.n commits not yet pushed / pulledThe usual case.No local changes / n local changesWhat has not been committed.n conflictsA pull found changes that could not be merged automatically. Until that is resolved, no push.No upstreamThe branch has no counterpart on the server. How many commits are missing therefore cannot be said — the first push creates it.No branch checked outThe project sits on a single commit. Push and pull have no target that way.No git repositoryA valid situation too. Sync is then not possible here.
What a sync does
The sentence stands above the buttons and is to be taken literally:

Every sync first commits your changes (when enabled below), then fetches the branch from
origin and pushes your current branch — as a force push, which is what the Quartz CLI does.

Three points about it matter:

The committing can be switched off. Without it, only the already committed state is moved. The
card says how many local changes would be affected.
Pull always fetches the same branch from origin — regardless of which one is checked out here.
On another branch the pull either fails or mixes something foreign in; the app then warns with both
names.
The push is a force push. That is the Quartz CLI’s behaviour, and it means: what is on the
server is replaced by the local state.

Push, pull and both together are three separate buttons.
Creating a repository
If there is none on GitHub yet, the card Create repository on GitHub creates one and enters it as
origin. That needs a token with the repo permission; without
one the app says where it belongs.
On the question of public or private see 6.2 — on the free plan,
private and Pages are mutually exclusive.
On the second machine
After cloning, two things are missing that deliberately do not live in the repository:

The dependencies — the first build reports it.
The built plugin files — fetched back under
Plugins → Maintenance.

And one is missing permanently: the snapshots. They belong to this
copy on this machine.

en/6-publishing/04-to-a-webspace.title: 6.4 To a webspace
en/6-publishing/04-to-a-webspace.content:
The classic route: the built files move into a folder on a server. Three methods are on offer, and the
difference is not only speed.
SFTP
Transfers file by file over an encrypted connection. Works with every provider offering SSH.
What matters is how SFTP knows what has changed: from a local list of what this app uploaded last.
Files somebody changes or deletes directly on the server go unnoticed.
rsync
Asks the server itself what is there. So the comparison holds even when somebody changed something
there by hand — and the transfer is faster.
Requirement: rsync has to be installed on the server. And on this page there are five reasons it can
be blocked; the app names whichever applies each time:





























ReasonWhat to doNo suitable connection chosenrsync needs SSH with a key file or an SSH agent.Password authenticationNot possible — ssh cannot take the password. Switch to a key.Key pasted as textrsync needs it as a file. Change the connection.Host key not confirmed yetPublish over SFTP once — the fingerprint is asked for then — after which rsync can be chosen.rsync missing on this machineOn Debian and Ubuntu: sudo apt install rsync.
In every one of those cases the same sentence applies: SFTP transfers the same files until then,
only without the comparison against the server.
FTP
The old route, and the app warns clearly:

FTP sends the password and all files in the clear. Without FTPS anyone on the same network can
read along — enable it if your provider supports it (or use SFTP instead).

If the provider supports FTPS, switch it on. Better still: use SFTP.
The remote path

The form for a new target; the type at the top decides which fields appear below.
The folder on the server the site goes into — httpdocs, say, or /var/www/example.com. Without a
leading slash it counts from the login directory; on a webspace that is the normal case.
Three inputs the app refuses:

Empty — without a target folder nothing can be published.
The login directory itself — with deletion enabled it would be emptied.
A path with ..

Authentication

A new SFTP connection, created from the target.
On the connection: password, private key or SSH agent.
With the SSH agent the app stores nothing at all — the key stays in the system’s agent. The
requirement is that it is reachable; in a session without an agent it does not work.
A password or a pasted key lives encrypted in the system’s
keychain.

en/6-publishing/05-to-a-folder.title: 6.5 To a folder
en/6-publishing/05-to-a-folder.content:
A target of type Folder copies the built site into a folder on this machine. No connection, no
network, no login.
That sounds like little and is the most useful way out this page has. It fits everywhere something
else takes over afterwards:

A folder a cloud service synchronises.
A mounted network drive.
A folder a script or a cron job of your own processes further.
A folder you simply want to look at or upload by hand.
A web server on the same machine.

What applies
The same rules as for the other targets: the content of the
output folder is transferred, the preview shows beforehand what
has changed, and Delete removed files in the target too is a decision of its own.
The exclusions apply here as well — see 6.7.

en/6-publishing/06-webhook.title: 6.6 Webhook
en/6-publishing/06-webhook.content:
A target of type Webhook transfers no files. It calls a URL and thereby asks a provider to
build the site itself — Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, a CI system.
What that changes
There is no file list here. No diff, no count of uploaded files, no progress over files — the
build runs there, not here. The app says so on the card itself.
The confirmation question is correspondingly short:

Trigger the webhook “…”?
No files are transferred — the provider is only asked to build on its own.

Where the URL comes from
From the provider. It lives on the connection, not on the target, because it is a credential:
whoever has it can trigger builds. It therefore lives in the
keychain like a password.
If no URL is stored on the connection, the target says so — “no URL stored” — instead of failing on
the click.
What the provider needs
For the build to find anything there, the provider has to reach the sources — usually through the
repository. So the usual sequence is: first
git sync, then trigger the webhook.

en/6-publishing/07-what-gets-uploaded.title: 6.7 What gets uploaded
en/6-publishing/07-what-gets-uploaded.content:
Before every transfer there is a list. It answers the question you have before the click — what
happens next?
The changes

Before the first diff, this says what to do: build or refresh.
The card Changes compares the current build with what last went to this target, and splits
into three groups: New, Changed, Removed.
If it says “No diff computed yet”, the comparison is missing: build first, or Refresh diff. If
it says “No changes since the last deploy”, there is nothing to do.
How reliable that list is depends on the method — see 6.4. rsync
asks the server; SFTP, FTP and the folder compare against a local list.
Upload everything again
The button for when the local list no longer holds. It discards what the app last sent to this target
— after which the preview offers the whole build again.
It is meant for everything the app cannot see: a file deleted on the server by hand, an aborted
transfer, a restore by the provider.
Delete removed files in the target too
A switch on the target. For good reason not a default but a decision:

On — whatever disappears from the build disappears on the server too. Tidy, but dangerous if
something else lives there.
Off — removed files stay. The app then adds that they keep being counted.

Never publish
One path per line, on the target. Whatever matches is not transferred and not touched when deleting —
.htaccess, say, or a stats/ folder the provider fills itself.
Not to be confused with the exclusions under
Configuration: those keep a note from becoming a page at
all. These keep a built file from reaching the server.
The output folder
It is the same as under Preview & build — what is uploaded
is what lies there. Change it in either place and you change it in both.
The confirmation
Before transferring, the app asks with numbers:

Publish to …?
34 file(s) will be uploaded, 2 file(s) will be deleted on the server.

For a branch target it says instead the sentence that matters:
the branch is replaced wholesale by the current build.

en/6-publishing/index.title: 6 Publishing
en/6-publishing/index.content:
A connection is a login with a provider and belongs to the app. A target belongs to a project
and says where its result should go. That distinction carries the whole chapter.
The pages of this chapter

6.1 Connections and targets — the difference, and
where each is set up.
6.2 GitHub Pages — from “no repository yet” to your own domain
over HTTPS.
6.3 Git sync — backing up the project itself and getting it onto a
second machine.
6.4 To a webspace — SFTP, rsync and FTP: what separates the
three.
6.5 To a folder — the route for everything another program
takes over afterwards.
6.6 Webhook — when the provider builds it itself.
6.7 What gets uploaded — the preview before the
transfer, exclusions, deletion behaviour.

en/7-maintenance/01-snapshots.title: 7.1 Snapshots
en/7-maintenance/01-snapshots.content:
A snapshot is a copy of this project that only this app knows
about. It stays inside the project, is never uploaded, and does not touch your own git history.

The backups page with the list of snapshots.
A snapshot is not git sync
The difference is at the very top of the page, because it is the most common misunderstanding:

























SnapshotGit syncFor whatfor going backfor sharingWhere tostays on this machineto GitHub, and from there to other machinesNeedsnothing — works even when the project is no repository at alla repository
The two do not exclude each other. You can and should use both.
What a snapshot holds
Everything that is yours in this project: the configuration, the plugins’ lock file, the
frames, your own stylesheets, the translations, the
publishing targets.
Not included: the dependencies, the build folder and the installed plugin files — those come about
again on the next build anyway.

The content folder is a switch of its own — locked here, because it is linked.
The content folder is a switch of its own, and that
depends on how it is built:

Real folder: can be included, and the app recommends it — Markdown is small enough to always
come along.
Linked: cannot be included. The snapshot holds the link, not
a single note. The vault is a source of its own with a backup of its own — and a snapshot would
never overwrite it anyway.

When one comes about on its own
Before every larger change, and the list is in the app too:

before a core update
before a plugin change
before a content switch
before importing a template package
before a restore
before a configuration change

Every snapshot carries its origin as a label — By you, Before core update, Before plugin change
and so on. That keeps the list readable when twenty of them are in it.
Ones you take yourself can be given a name: “before the theme switch” is worth more in three
weeks than a timestamp.
Comparing
Compare puts a snapshot against today’s state: how many files differ, and for each the textual
difference. Three states per file — changed, added since, deleted since.
With a linked vault the app adds what the comparison does not cover: everything except the content
folder.
Exporting
Export as ZIP puts a snapshot down as an ordinary file — for an archive outside the project, or to
send to somebody.

en/7-maintenance/02-restoring.title: 7.2 Restoring
en/7-maintenance/02-restoring.content:
Two routes lead back out of a snapshot, and they differ in
thoroughness.
Single files
In the comparison, files can be selected and only those reset. The usual case: a stylesheet broke
yesterday, everything else should stay.
The whole project
Restore everything resets the project to the snapshot’s state. The sentence in the question is the
important one:

Files that did not exist back then will be deleted.

So a restore is not an addition but a return. Whatever came about since is gone afterwards — unless it
is in a later snapshot.
There is always a way back from going back
A snapshot of the current state is taken automatically first. That is in both questions, and it
means: even an accidental restore can be undone. The new snapshot carries the label Before restore.
The special case: undoing a core update
Restoring offers an extra switch: Also reset the project commit.
It is needed in exactly one case — when a core update is to be undone.
Without it the files would come back, but the project’s git history would stay at the new state, and
the updates page would keep reporting everything as current.
One note on it is meant seriously: if that commit has already been pushed, the local state then
diverges from the server. That is to be sorted out before the next
sync.
What a restore does not bring back
The vault, when the content folder is
linked. It was never in the snapshot; the app says afterwards
explicitly that its files were left untouched and that everything outside the content folder has been
restored.

en/7-maintenance/03-updates.title: 7.3 Updates
en/7-maintenance/03-updates.content:
Two things can be updated, and they sit in two cards: the Quartz core and the plugins.

Updates for the core and the plugins.
Three answers, not two
The state of a check is Current, Update available — or Cannot check. The last means neither
of the other two: the question did not get through. Check again tries once more.
The core

The installed and the latest state of the core.
The card names the installed and the latest state. Run update asks first, and the question has
three parts:

Update Quartz’s core?
This fetches changes from jackyzha0/quartz and reinstalls the dependencies; conflicts may require
manual work.
A snapshot is taken first — under Backups you can go back to the current state any time.

The last sentence is the safety net. What a snapshot holds is
in 7.1.
When there are conflicts
A core update is a merge of two states. Where both sides changed the same file, a conflict comes about,
and the page lists the affected files.
Two ways out sit right beside it:

Abort merge — back to the state from before.
Open the snapshot from before the update — the route via
restoring, including the switch for the project commit.

Your own translations are excluded when their update protection is set up — the list says so
explicitly. Anyone with wording of their own should check the protection beforehand, see
3.5.
The plugins

Only what came in through the marketplace or by hand.
The second card shows only plugins added through the marketplace or by hand. The built-in ones —
in a new project, most of them — are updated automatically with the core above.
Individually or all together. Here too a snapshot is taken first.
A plugin with an available update carries the badge in the plugin list as
well.
The app itself
A newer version of QuartzControl is reported by the start screen, with both version numbers and a
link. It downloads nothing and changes nothing — updating the app is the same route as installing it,
see 1.3.

en/7-maintenance/04-cleaning-up.title: 7.4 Cleaning up
en/7-maintenance/04-cleaning-up.content:
Four things accumulate over time. Three of them may go, one only with care.
Set-aside content folders
Switching the content folder does not lose the previous one: it is
set aside rather than deleted, and the backups page lists it. From there it can be put back or
deleted for good.


                  
                  That is the only copy 
                  
                

On deleting, the app says so clearly: a set-aside folder is not included in the
snapshots, and it cannot be undone.


And once more, because it is the most common misunderstanding: this is not a backup of your notes.
If the content folder was a link to a
vault, nothing was ever copied — only the link was recorded.
Old snapshots
They live in the project and grow with it. Deletable individually; the question about it is short,
because deleting a snapshot changes nothing about today’s state.
If you need space, delete the oldest and keep the ones with a name — those were taken for a reason.
Built plugin files
Under Plugins → Maintenance: Remove orphaned plugin folders deletes
whatever no configuration points at any more. The configuration itself stays unchanged — nothing the
site needs is lost.
The counterpart beside it, Restore from quartz.lock.json, fetches them back.
The theme cache
In the settings under Data & maintenance: the labels of the theme
options, fetched from GitHub once and kept. Clear cache forces a fresh load.
The only reason for it is that a theme changed its descriptions and the app still shows the old ones.
The cache takes up hardly any space; the card names the number of entries and the size.
The build folder
It is emptied and refilled completely on every
build — so there is nothing to tidy there. Anyone wanting it
gone for good deletes it; the next build creates it again.

en/7-maintenance/index.title: 7 Maintenance
en/7-maintenance/index.content:
Everything in this chapter serves one question: how do I get back when something goes wrong?
The pages of this chapter

7.1 Snapshots — what one holds, when the app takes one on its
own, and why a snapshot is not git sync.
7.2 Restoring — a whole project or a single file, and what
disappears in the process.
7.3 Updates — updating the Quartz core and the plugins, and what
to do about a conflict.
7.4 Cleaning up — set-aside content folders, built plugin
files, caches.

en/8-reference/01-glossary.title: Glossary
en/8-reference/01-glossary.content:
A reference, not a read. Wherever a term first appears on a page in this handbook, a link points
here.
How to write notes — callouts, bases, canvases, frontmatter fields — is explained by the
handbook of the example template Example, which has a larger glossary of its own. What follows is
what the app itself says.
Base URL
The address the finished site will be reachable at, without https:// — notes.example.com, say.
Quartz builds every link, the RSS feed and the preview images from it. Set under Setup →
Configuration; while it is unknown, localhost stays.
Branch
One strand in a repository’s history. A project always
sits on exactly one; push and pull refer to it. When publishing via GitHub Pages the target branch
is usually gh-pages and pointedly not the one you work on — it is replaced wholesale on every
deploy.
Build
The process in which Quartz turns the content folder
into a finished website: Markdown becomes HTML, plus a search index, a graph and stylesheets. The
result lands in an output folder, usually public. Every build empties that folder first —
which is why the app asks when something in there does not look like a build.
Commit
A saved state in a repository’s history, with a date, an
author and a description. A snapshot is technically one
too — but in a history of its own that only the app knows about.
Community theme
A ready-made colour scheme from the @quartz-themes ecosystem, installed and activated under
Design → Community themes. It sits in the second of the four layers: it overrides the base colours,
and is overridden in turn by your own CSS variables and your own CSS.
Connection
A login with a provider: server, username, password or key. A connection belongs to the app, not to
a project — the same webspace account can carry several sites, and a password change is then one
change rather than one per project.
Content folder
The content/ folder in the project, holding the Markdown files the site is built from. It is
either a real folder or a link to a folder outside the
project — to a vault, for instance.
CSS variable
A named value a stylesheet uses in many places — a colour, a spacing, a font size. Change it once
and everything using it changes. Quartz derives many variables from a few base colours; the
Variables tab shows, for each one, where its value comes from and what depends on it.
Dev server
A program that builds the site, serves it at http://localhost:<port> and rebuilds on every change
to a note. The preview in QuartzControl is exactly that. It keeps running when the window is
closed, and is never stopped on its own.
Frame
The grid of a page: which areas exist — header, sidebars, content, footer —, where they sit and how
wide they are. Quartz brings three (default, full-width, minimal); your own are built in the layout
editor, for three screen widths each. What appears in those areas is decided by another tab.
Frontmatter
The block between two lines of three dashes at the very top of a Markdown file. It holds the title,
description, date, tags and everything else a page says about itself.
Git sync
Reconciling the project with a repository — uploading
(push) and downloading (pull). Meant for sharing and for the second machine. Not to be confused
with a snapshot, which is for going back, nor with
publishing, which sends the finished site.
Host key
The fingerprint a server identifies itself with when connecting over SFTP or rsync. The first time,
the app asks and remembers it. If it changes later, the app stops: that can be a freshly set-up
server — or somebody in between.
Keychain
The operating system’s encrypted store for passwords (macOS: Keychain, Windows: Credential Manager,
Linux: gnome-keyring or KWallet). QuartzControl puts passwords and tokens there, not in a file of
its own. Where one is missing on a Linux system, the start screen says so explicitly.
Link
An entry in the filesystem pointing at another folder without copying it — a symbolic link,
technically. The content folder can be built that
way: it then is the vault, and whoever writes there writes
at the source.
Markdown
A plain way of writing text in which **bold** becomes bold and # Heading a heading. Every note
is a text file ending in .md.
Marketplace
The list of plugins from the quartz-community organisation on GitHub, searchable and installable
with one click. Plugins from elsewhere are added via owner/repo.
Page type
A kind of page Quartz distinguishes: the ordinary content page, the start page, a tag page, a
folder page. Each page type can be given a frame of its own.
Part
One piece of a template package. There are twelve:
colours and fonts, community theme, plugins, layout, frames, presets, translations, stylesheets,
fonts, static files, CSS variables and the content. Each is picked or left out individually, on
export as on import.
What appears on the page is a plugin or a component
instead — until 2026-09-07 the app called that a “part” in one place too.
Plugin
A building block of Quartz with one job: one builds the explorer on the left, one the table of
contents on the right, one the search, one reads a file’s date. Some appear visibly on the page,
others only change the content behind the scenes. Which are active and how they are configured is
in quartz.config.yaml.
Preset
A saved set of theme settings under a name of its own. Useful for keeping two colour worlds side by
side without losing the first.
Project
A folder holding a Quartz installation: the configuration, the
content folder, the stylesheets, the plugins.
QuartzControl can manage several; everything except the start screen and the settings applies to
one of them.
Publishing
Getting the finished site to where it belongs — via GitHub Pages, SFTP, rsync, FTP, into a folder
or through a webhook. Two things belong to it: a connection
and a target.
Quartz
The static site generator this app drives. It
understands Obsidian’s notation and builds a site with backlinks, a graph view and full-text search.
Repository
A folder whose history git records. If it also lives on a server — GitHub, say — it can be used
from several machines.
Snapshot
A copy of this project that only QuartzControl knows about. It stays inside the project, is never
uploaded, and does not touch your own git history. The app takes one on its own before every larger
change; you can restore the whole project or a single file.
Static site generator
A program that turns a folder full of text files into a folder full of finished HTML pages. The
result needs no database and no program on the server — it simply sits there and is served.
Target
Where this project publishes to: the server path, the deletion behaviour, the exclusions — and
which connection is used for it. A target belongs to a
project.
Template package
A single file ending in .qtpl holding a project’s design — colours, theme, stylesheets, fonts,
layout, frames, plugins, translations — and carrying it into another project. Assembled from twelve
parts that can be picked and left out individually.
Token
A password substitute for an interface, here: for GitHub. Without one the
marketplace is exhausted after a few requests; creating a
repository and using GitHub Pages additionally needs the repo permission.
Vault
A folder full of notes, as Obsidian manages it. A
content folder can point straight at one — then you
write in Obsidian and the site follows.
Wikilink
A link in double square brackets, [[like this]], the way Obsidian writes it. Quartz resolves it at
build time. How the targets are written — shortest form, absolute or relative — has to match your
notes in the configuration, or the links find nothing.

en/8-reference/02-menu-and-shortcuts.title: Menu and shortcuts
en/8-reference/02-menu-and-shortcuts.content:
The menu is deliberately small. Almost everything happens in the interface; the menu has four jobs
that are hard to place there.
The three shortcuts that matter





















ShortcutWhat it does⌘S / Ctrl+SSaves the open page — the same as the save button.⌘, / Ctrl+,Opens the settings.⌘Q / Ctrl+QQuits the app. What happens to a running dev server is in the settings.
⌘S only acts where there is something to save. On a page without a document it does nothing — and
that is precisely why the menu entry is never greyed out.
The menus
File — Save, and on Windows and Linux additionally Settings and Quit. On macOS those two live in
the application menu, where they belong.
Edit — Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All. The system’s usual commands, for the text fields
in the app.
View — Reload, Developer tools, Zoom, Full screen. The zoom is the most useful of them: it
enlarges the whole interface.
Window — Minimise, Zoom, and on macOS “Bring All to Front”.
Help — five entries:

Handbook — this one, from the beginning. It travels with the app and opens in the browser; it
needs no network, and it always matches the version installed. The same route sits on the start
screen beside the two links below it — and anyone looking for a particular page had better use
“Read this in the handbook” in the header of the screen they are on: that leads straight to the
matching chapter.
Send feedback — opens a prepared message.
Quartz documentation — where this handbook stops.
Plugin catalogue — the organisation on GitHub.
Open data folder — see Where the data lives.

What the menu cannot do
Anything project-related. You switch projects in the sidebar via All projects, not through a menu
— there is no “recently opened” list there, because the start screen is one.
Keyboard operation in the interface
Two places deserve a mention of their own, because they replace a gesture otherwise known only with a
mouse:
Dragging and dropping works everywhere with the keyboard: pick up with space or enter, move with
the arrow keys, drop with space or enter, cancel with escape. That covers the plugin list, the
frame editor and the layout board. Sortable rows additionally carry
move up and move down.
Switch bars — the tabs under the header, the choice between light and dark, the preview width —
are radio groups: one tab stop leads in, the arrow keys change the selection, wrapping at both ends.

en/8-reference/03-where-the-data-lives.title: Where the data lives
en/8-reference/03-where-the-data-lives.content:
QuartzControl puts things in three places. Knowing them also tells you what a backup has to cover.
In the project
Everything that makes up the site — and a few things that only concern the app:









































WhatTravels with the project?quartz.config.yaml, stylesheets, language filesyesThe plugins’ lock fileyesYour own framesyesThe project imageyesThe snapshotsno — they belong to this copy on this machineSet-aside content foldersnoThe built plugin filesno — restorable from the lock fileThe dependencies and the build folderno — they come about again
“Travels with” means: lives in a repository, when the project
lives in one.
In the app’s data folder
The project list, the settings and the connections —
everything that does not belong to a single project.
Where that folder is is in the settings under Data & maintenance,
with a button that opens it; the same is available via Help → Open data folder.
The theme documentation cache lives there too, and — where needed — the runtime environment the app
rewrites on every start.
In the system’s keychain
Passwords, keys and tokens. Not in a file of the app’s: they
live encrypted in the operating system’s
keychain.
Which also means: they travel with no backup — neither with the project nor with the data folder.
On a new machine the connections have to be entered again; a project’s
targets are then there, but without a login.
On Linux this depends on a running keychain. Where one is missing, the
start screen says so explicitly instead of pretending everything
is encrypted.
In the app itself
This handbook. It lies as a finished website inside the app, so it is installed with it and updated
with it — it cannot go stale while the app is current, and it needs no network. Reachable via
Help → Handbook or from the start screen.
When one of these files is unreadable
If the app cannot read one of its own files at startup, it sets it aside rather than overwriting
it — so the content is still there. What it held is missing from the app, and the settings report it
under Data & maintenance.

en/8-reference/04-known-limits.title: Known limits
en/8-reference/04-known-limits.content:
More honest than a feature list: what is here was checked against the app while writing this handbook.
What the app pointedly does not do
It is not an editor. Notes are written elsewhere. QuartzControl reads the
content folder and does not touch its content.
It never kills a foreign process on its own. A dev server
started by a terminal is listed but stopped only on an explicit decision — see
5.4.
It does not write into somebody else’s vault. If content/ is a
link, importing a
template package skips the content part.
It gives no all-clear it cannot measure. Cannot check, unknown and CSS unchecked are answers
of their own and never mean “fine”.
What it cannot do





























































LimitWay outNo Windows package — macOS (dmg, zip) and Linux (AppImage, deb) are shipped—The macOS app is unsigned; the first launch is refusedStart it once with right click → OpenOne window only; two projects cannot be open side by sideSwitch between themA snapshot does not back up a linked vaultBack up the vault itselfSnapshots do not travel with the projectOn the second machine the list starts emptyCredentials travel with no backup — they live in the keychainEnter them again on a new machineOn Linux without a keychain the encryption is only formalSet up gnome-keyring or KWalletrsync does not work with password authenticationKey file or SSH agent, see 6.4Bundled plugins ship no option descriptionsAdd values by hand; the names are in the plugin’s repositoryA frame from a plugin gets no preview—A component placed more than once can only be hidden together per page type—Variables a theme sets only inside an element cannot be overridden globallyCustom CSSA theme without colour settings of its own cannot be configured hereVariables or custom CSS
This handbook is bilingual, the interface around it is not
On an English page of this handbook, “Inhaltsverzeichnis”, “Graphansicht”, “Zuletzt bearbeitete
Seiten” and the search’s labels stay in German. That is not a forgotten translation: Quartz’s
components read the site’s language, not the language of the page they are building — checked in
the built code of the explorer and the backlinks, not guessed. The same holds for the search index,
“last modified”, the global graph and the single 404.html.
One of those can be moved: dates are reformatted in the browser in the page’s language. Everything
else takes a build per language — at the price of two addresses.
The handbook of the example template Example shows the same behaviour, so the limit is not this
site’s doing.
Where the boundary to Quartz runs
Much of what stands out on the finished page is decided not by this app but by Quartz or a
plugin: what becomes of an Obsidian drawing, which task states
survive, how a diagram is rendered, what the explorer sorts by.
Two addresses for that:

The handbook of the example template Example — it shows, for every element, what becomes of it,
and keeps a list of known limits of its own.
The Quartz documentation.

When something is missing
Help → Send feedback opens a prepared message.
